records.sourceFile: Acute effects of ad libitum use of commercially available cannabis products on the subjective experience of aerobic exercise - A crossover study.pdf

paper.citation: Gibson LP, Giordano GR, Bidwell LC, Hutchison KE, Bryan AD. Acute Effects of Ad Libitum Use of Commercially Available Cannabis Products on the Subjective Experience of Aerobic Exercise: A Crossover Study. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: Regular cannabis users ran for 30 minutes on a treadmill once after ad libitum use of a THC-dominant or CBD-dominant cannabis flower product and once without cannabis. Cannabis runs were rated more positively, with more enjoyment, positive affect and runner's high symptoms, but also with more perceived exertion. The size of some effects differed by product, and the authors urge caution in interpreting these differences given the small groups.
paper.tldr: In regular cannabis users running on a treadmill, cannabis before exercise increased enjoyment, positive mood and runner's high symptoms, but also perceived exertion, with the exertion increase seen mainly after the THC-dominant product. The study had no placebo arm, a small CBD group and no performance outcome.
paper.methods: Laboratory crossover study. Forty-two regular cannabis users (28 men, 12 women, 2 non-binary; about 383 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise per week) who had used cannabis while running completed a baseline Talk Test to set a treadmill speed and incline near the ventilatory threshold, then two 30-minute runs at least 48 hours apart in randomized order: one without cannabis and one about 33 minutes after ad libitum home use of an assigned flower product (THC-dominant, 24% THC and 1% CBD, or CBD-dominant, 1% THC and 20% CBD). Products were allocated by a die roll that participants could decline, and exertion, pain, affect, arousal, enjoyment and runner's high were rated during or after each run and analysed with mixed-effects models.
paper.findings: Cannabis runs were rated higher for affective valence, enjoyment and runner's high symptoms (all P<0.001). Exertion was higher on cannabis runs overall (B=0.32, P=0.04), with the difference present in the THC group (P<0.001) and not the CBD group (P=0.93). The enjoyment and affect differences were larger in the CBD group (interaction P=0.02 and P=0.003), and resting heart rate was higher before cannabis exercise in the THC group only (P<0.001). Pain was very low on both runs (about 1 out of 10), and %HRmax did not differ overall (P=0.15).
paper.limitations: Participants knew their product, and the groups were unbalanced (31 THC, 11 CBD) after several CBD-assigned participants switched to THC and CBD attrition was slightly higher, so the product comparisons are underpowered. There was no placebo and participants held favourable beliefs about cannabis with exercise (90.5% said it increased enjoyment), so expectancy and prior experience cannot be separated from drug effects; heart rate was available for only 31 participants and pain scores were at a floor. The text has internal inconsistencies: mean plasma THC in the THC group is 114 ng/mL in Table 2 but 148 ng/mL in the Discussion, and the Figure 3 note gives a 1 to 6 range for affective valence although the Feeling Scale runs from -5 to +5; table values were used.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who discuss cannabis use around training with athletes can note that, in this sample, cannabis before a run changed how the run felt, with more enjoyment and some extra effort. The study measured no performance benefit, so it does not support cannabis for improving training or competition, and its safety for athletes was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: In this sample, cannabis before running changed how the run felt, with more enjoyment and some extra effort after the THC-dominant product, but no performance outcome was measured. The study does not show a training benefit.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It excluded people with musculoskeletal problems or injuries that limit exercise, and it studied neither injured athletes nor recovery, so its low pain findings should not be used to support cannabis for pain after injury.
